extracted.intended_audience: patent litigators, IP attorneys, patent prosecutors, in-house counsel, and patent examiners
extracted.subtask_description: A compilation of post-Alice case holdings used to evaluate whether patent claims are directed to patent‑ineligible subject matter under 35 U.S.C. §101 (Alice two-step): (1) whether claims are directed to an abstract idea and (2) whether they nonetheless contain an inventive concept. The chart summarizes recurring legal criteria and examples from Federal Circuit, district court, and PTAB decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Directed to an abstract idea
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims are ineligible if they are 'directed to the abstract idea' — e.g., collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying results; delivering user-selected media; transaction performance guaranty; organizing market information; cataloging labor data; indexing and searching data; encoding/decoding image data; rules for playing games; other fundamental concepts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chart repeatedly labels claims as 'directed to the abstract idea' with many concrete formulations from cases (e.g., 'collecting information, analyzing it, and displaying certain results of the collection and analysis'; 'the abstract idea of showing an advertisement before delivering free content'; 'abstract idea of conditioning and controlling access to data based on payment'; 'a loan-application clearinghouse'; 'graphing trading data to assist a trader'). Use these formulations to map a claim to familiar abstract-idea categories: data collection/organization/analysis/display; fundamental economic practices; mental processes/rules; mathematical concepts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lack of inventive concept
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims fail step two of Alice when they 'lack an inventive concept' — i.e., when the claim elements add nothing 'significantly more' than the abstract idea and instead recite only generic, conventional components or steps.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples from the chart: courts held claims 'lacked an inventive concept because they merely recited generic computer components' (interface, network, database, server, telephone unit); 'use of a scanner ... was well-known'; 'addition of conventional computer components to business practices' is insufficient. When assessing inventive concept, examine whether claim elements transform the abstract idea into a technical improvement or merely append conventional technology.

rubrics_metrics.name: Generic computer implementation is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Reciting implementation on a computer or 'software instructions without any hardware limitations' does not make an abstract idea patent eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chart contains many holdings that 'merely implement[ed] an old practice in a new environment' or that claims 'required only generic computer components functioning in their conventional manner.' Courts distinguish claims that improve computer functionality from those that merely use computers as tools. Look for specific hardware/software limitations and whether they meaningfully constrict the abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must be directed to an improvement in computer/technology functioning to be eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that are 'directed to an improvement in computer technology' (or solve a technological problem in computers/networks) can be eligible, whereas claims that simply apply abstract ideas using computers are not.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chart contrasts eligible and ineligible decisions, noting that claims unlike those in DDR Holdings, Enfish, or McRO — i.e., claims not 'rooted in computer technology' and not showing an 'improvement in computer or network functionality' — are ineligible. Assess whether the claim recites a technical solution or an improvement in how computers operate, not merely an application of a business/abstract idea.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mathematical equations or mere data transformations alone do not confer eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The 'addition of a mathematical equation that simply changes the data into other forms of data' does not supply an inventive concept or render the claim eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case holdings note that mathematical manipulation or converting data formats without a technical improvement is insufficient. Evaluate whether mathematical steps are tied to a technical application that improves computing or are merely abstract calculations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty/nonobviousness under §§102/103 are not substitutes for §101 eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: It 'is not enough for subject-matter eligibility that claimed techniques be novel and nonobvious in light of prior art' — an advance that lies entirely in the realm of abstract ideas remains ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: SAP Am. v. InvestPic and other summaries emphasize that passing §§102/103 does not cure §101 problems. When advising clients, separate the §101 analysis from novelty/nonobviousness arguments; technical improvements matter for §101, not merely field-specific advances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preemption concerns inform eligibility analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts treat preemption as related to §101 — claims that risk preempting use of an abstract idea across its practical applications support ineligibility findings ('preemption concerns are fully addressed and made moot' when claims are ineligible).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use preemption as an indicator: broad claims that would monopolize an abstract idea (e.g., all ways of conducting a basic economic practice) are especially likely to be held ineligible. However, courts analyze substance (directed-to/inventive-concept) rather than preemption alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factual disputes about conventionality can affect the §101 inquiry
rubrics_metrics.description: Following Berkheimer, whether claim elements are 'well-understood, routine, and conventional' can be a factual question that may preclude resolution at the pleading or summary-judgment stage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The chart records cases remanded or reversed where factual evidence (e.g., specification disclosures, extrinsic evidence) raised disputes about conventionality. Note, however, that some judges (e.g., Judge Mayer) dissent and dispute that §101 should involve fact questions. Treat conventionality evidence carefully: it can create triable issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that merely state resulting systems/functionality without specific programming/design are insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that 'merely claim the resulting systems' or 'functionality' and fail to 'claim a particular way of programming or designing the software' are directed to an abstract idea and lack inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether claims specify how the software/hardware achieves the result (specific architecture, unconventional steps) rather than simply claiming the end result or function. Many cases reject claims that restate functions at a high level of generality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statements of advantage or business benefit do not establish eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: A claimed 'advantage' (e.g., better business outcomes) is not the standard for subject-matter eligibility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Case law in the chart expressly states that an asserted advantage does not make an otherwise abstract claim patent eligible. Focus on technical character, not commercial benefit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion of conventional hardware or identifiers does not render claim eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Adding known hardware components or identifiers (e.g., tags, basic hardware identifiers) without more does not create an inventive concept; courts have held there was 'no indication that their inclusion produce[d] a result that overrides the routine and conventional use' of the hardware.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine whether hardware elements are novel or used in a non-conventional way producing a technical improvement. Mere presence of generic hardware (interfaces, servers, databases, cellular phone features) is usually insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must recite how data is transformed to show a technical contribution
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that gather and output data but 'did not recite how data was transformed in any way' were held ineligible because they fail to show a technical manner of transformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims process data, identify concrete transformational steps (e.g., changing data representation in a way that improves technology) rather than mere collection/printing/displaying. Lack of transformation detail often supports finding of abstractness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rules for playing games or pure human activity organization are abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting 'rules for playing a dice game' or methods of managing/playing games (e.g., bingo) have been treated as abstract ideas and held ineligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat game rules, mental steps, and other pure organizational methods as paradigmatic abstract ideas unless tied to a technical improvement in computing or other statutory category.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims directed to fundamental economic practices are abstract
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims involving fundamental economic concepts — e.g., loan-application clearinghouses, financial instruments, auction payment mechanics, conditioning access on payment, pricing/advertising strategies — are routinely characterized as abstract ideas.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Financial/business-method claims must show a technical solution or improvement beyond the mere economic practice implemented on conventional systems to survive §101 scrutiny.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that cover non-tangible/non-physical items may fall outside statutory categories
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have pointed out that items 'not a tangible or physical thing' (e.g., a 'device profile' as described in Digitech) 'do not fall within any of the categories of eligible subject matter.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims focus on purely intangible constructs without physical transformation or concrete application, consider statutory-category issues (machine, manufacture, composition, or process) as well as abstractness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patent eligibility can be decided at Rule 12(b)(6) or Rule 12(c) when facts undisputedly show ineligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have repeatedly stated that, 'like other legal questions based on underlying facts,' subject-matter eligibility 'may be, and frequently has been, resolved on a Rule 12(b)(6) or (c) motion where the undisputed facts ... require a holding of ineligibility under the substantive standards of law.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the claim language and acceptably pleaded facts establish that the claims are directed to an abstract idea and lack inventive concept (and no factual disputes over conventionality exist), dismissal on the pleadings or summary judgment is appropriate. If factual disputes exist (see Berkheimer), proceed to fact development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Implementation that merely applies an abstract idea in a new environment is insufficient
rubrics_metrics.description: Courts have characterized claims that simply apply a known practice 'in a new environment' (e.g., implementing an old practice on the Internet) as ineligible when no technical improvement is claimed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ask whether the claim adds anything beyond relocating an abstract idea to a particular technological environment (e.g., 'on the Internet') — mere relocation without technical contribution fails §101.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that provide only high-level steps of conventional processes are ineligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting 'conventional steps, specified at a high level of generality' are inadequate to supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Look for specificity in how steps are performed and whether their ordering or combination produces a non-conventional technical result; blanket recitation of 'interfaces,' 'networks,' 'databases,' or 'generic steps' is usually insufficient.
